question.text: Jeevan Jyoti Foundation runs a charitable hospital in rural Maharashtra. Its annual receipts are INR 4.5 crore. The SIA is advising the board on the cleanest tax-exemption route. Under which provision can a charitable hospital claim exemption as a 'specified institution' subject to prescribed receipt limits, distinct from the Section 11 general charitable-trust route?

answer.text: Section 10(23C) — specified educational and medical institutions, subject to prescribed receipt thresholds
Section 80G — the institution itself becomes tax-exempt under 80G registration
Section 115BBI — exemption for anonymous donations above INR 1 lakh
Section 2(15) — exemption applies to any entity with a 'charitable purpose'

explanation.text: The Logic: Section 10(23C) of the Income Tax Act provides exemption to specified categories of institutions — notably educational institutions and hospitals existing solely for charitable/philanthropic purposes and not for profit — subject to prescribed receipt limits and approval from the prescribed authority. This is an alternative route to the Section 11 general charitable-trust exemption. Section 80G is donor-side; 115BBI is an anti-abuse rate; Section 2(15) merely defines 'charitable purpose'. The Trap: 80G is the donor's deduction, not the institution's exemption. 115BBI is a penalty rate on anonymous donations. Section 2(15) only provides the definition — it does not grant exemption. Cross-Exam Context: X-A/X-B (Investment Adviser) may touch 10(23C) when structuring HNI medical-trust advice. XXIII tests the SIA's ability to identify the correct exemption route during engagement scoping. Assessor's Pro-Tip: For 10(23C) institutions, the 'solely for philanthropic purposes' test is stricter than the Section 11 test — any significant commercial activity jeopardises the whole exemption. In your SAS-200 (healthcare) assessment, check the fee-waiver register vs paid-patient ratio to evidence the 'solely philanthropic' claim.
